utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will both parties make their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Tochilovsky, and I'm with Sureta Chana, Marie Tuma, Manoj Sachdeva, and Hasan Younis for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. My name is Mr. Morrissey, and I now appear for Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and with me appears Mr. Mettraux as counsel, and also I seek leave for Mr. Amir Cengic to appear to assist me as a legal assistant, who is on my far left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. This is the eighth Status Conference, which is held in accordance with Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The issue of counsel again arose in this case. However, I see that it has been now resolved with Mr. Peter Morrissey as the new lead counsel, and I welcome you, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As we are all aware, this case was ready for trial, and the trial was scheduled to take place in the middle of January this year. However, due to the lack of availability of a Trial Chamber to hear the case, this case was not to be. Thereafter, again due to the issue of counsel, progress to move this case to the trial was delayed again, and now that the issue of counsel has been resolved, can I take it that the case should be back on track to commence trial at any moment from now? May I first hear from the Defence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, as the Court pleases. Your Honour, the position as to the Defence is that we shall meet any deadlines that are required by the Court. We propose to be ready for any trial date that is set, and we shall met deadlines as required. May I indicate that there are, of course, some preferences that the Defence has, so far as the Court is concerned to hear those, that at all times our concern is to ensure that Mr. Halilovic is properly represented and that we're in a position to proceed quickly and efficiently when the trial begins. And as a result of that, we would be prepared to meet such speculative deadlines as have been set, but of course we would also be comfortable with an extended preparation time, should that be available. Now, therefore, the ideal from the Defence perspective, and it is simply the Defence perspective, not that of the Court, of all the parties necessarily, is that the trial commence at some time late in December or in January of the following year. However, we will meet earlier deadlines than that if called upon to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. Indeed, I'm very pleased to hear your responses and -- because this case is indeed on the top of the list of the Tribunal cases, ready to commence trial. I'm yet to be confirmed, but I was informed that there's a possibility in the Tribunal that for this case to start in December of this year or January next year, as you suggested, possibly after the case of Blagojevic. So please bear this in mind and make your preparations accordingly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that indication is very welcome and we can comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will -- let's deal with some pending motions, unless there's any observation from the Prosecution on the commencement of trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Nothing in addition to what was said at the previous Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There are several pending motions, I guess, some of which are outstanding for a substantial period of time. The first thing would be the Prosecution's Rule 92 bis motion, and in relation to which we have Defence response and addendum. However, it is my personal opinion that a final decision on this can be best made by the Trial Chamber which will actually hear the case in the future. But this is under review of this Chamber also, and parties will be informed in due course, in due manner, on this issue. We have another motion in relation regarding a subpoena from the Defence, which case was remitted from the Appeals Chamber, and I think I can inform you that decisions will be issued very shortly. And there's another motion from the Defence requesting for access to personnel files, and this is under consideration of the Trial Chamber and their decision will be rendered in due course. And the final motion, pending motion, will be the motion in relation to the disclosure of 66(A)(ii) materials and opposition from the Defence, which is also under review of the Trial Chamber. However, it involves some difficult issue, or some tricky issue, as to whether a Trial Chamber has the power to order the Prosecution to cease or to stop the investigation, and then the issue number two, possible sanction we can think of when Prosecution did not comply would be disallowing the material to be disclosed, but which may be to the contrary -- prejudicial to the Defence on the contrary. So the Chamber is reviewing this matter. However, I'm of the view that, also the Chamber, there should come a time for the Prosecution to complete their investigation if the case is ready to start. So having said that, with that in mind, can I turn to the Prosecution to ask the following two things: First, if Prosecution could elaborate reasons for the delayed disclosure for the last submission in relation to five witnesses, and then whether it is still going to re-investigate the case, or re-interview the witnesses, and going to disclose those materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just a few thoughts on issues which was just -- has been just raised. As to the right of the Prosecution to continue the investigation and whether the Prosecution should be -- or could be stopped from conducting it, I think one of the issues here is what is the investigation, what it means when Defence raised this issue. For instance, during trial some question may arise which would require the Prosecution to revisit a witness, to interview the witness or to interview new witness. Is it investigation during trial or, for instance, when you contact witness as we are supposed to do on a regular basis to keep contact with them, so when we have the order for trial we know where witnesses are and how they are prepared to go -- to come here. When you contact the witness and they provide you with some information which is relevant to the case, is it a new investigation? I think it should be made clear. The case is ready for trial, which means the major investigation, if I may say that, is completed. But I don't see how Prosecution can be prevented from -- I see only one situation where the Prosecution is prevented to speak to witnesses. It's when the witness takes the stand, started his testimony to the courtroom. This is the OTP practice. It's ICTY practice that neither party should contact witnesses. This is the only example I can see where Prosecution can be barred from contacting witnesses since speaking to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tochilovsky, I'm not minded going into some detailed discussion today. The first question was asked because of this: The Prosecution said it interviewed the witnesses, those five witnesses, again, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you elaborate on that. What points were elaborated by these new five witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I don't have the statements before me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: For those five witnesses or any other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was reminded that -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I was reminded by the Senior Legal Officer if necessary, we may go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: As you can see from Defence numerous submissions, the Defence is of course - it is natural - they prepared their case, they approach our witnesses, and some of our witnesses would say, you know, when we talk to them, they say, you know, we decided to testify for the Defence and we actually changed our statement. Of course, we would like to clarify. When we see, for instance, such a notice from the Defence, of course it's natural to contact the witness and clarify the matter. It's just one of the reasons why you would like to clarify the issue. Secondly, as you find or come across a witness, and he would provide you with information relevant to the case, it may prompt you to re-approach your witness you already interviewed if you obtained new information. Or the third -- anyway, there are various circumstances under which you would be prompted, you would have to approach your witnesses to clarify matters relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecution did make general submissions in your filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Usually it can be -- it's -- I would say it is a case by case issue. For instance, when you read the statement, additional statement, it's always can be seen from the statement itself why it was taken. It usually short statement from the question asked the witness is immediately clear what was the purpose of this interview and what was the purpose of this clarification. For instance, just another example. There are two potential witnesses who are not on our witness list but known to the Defence. We disclosed everything to the Defence relevant to those witnesses. Those who committed crimes within this indictment who are under investigation and prosecution are even convicted in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who are now, after they have been convicted or charged, willing to cooperate with us. Of course we will approach those witnesses. And I don't see that there's a new -- a re-investigation of the case. Both the Defence would benefit from them because it clarified the case not only for the Prosecution. It clarified the case for the Defence, it clarified the case for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's come into a specific question. At this moment, does the Prosecution have a specific plan to have more interviews and have more witness statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I would say there are issues which are, to put it simply, protected under 66(C), which is -- if we have obligation to disclose, we would approach Trial Chamber if the facts are investigation [sic]. For instance, in other cases but relevant to this case. But in general terms, we are not envisaging for the interviews except for maybe one which may happen within a month or even shorter period of time. Again, I cannot name the potential witness. I cannot name the person, because it is a pending investigation. All I can say, that just refer to example I provided before. When person is arrested, like Sakrak or others in Bosnia and is willing to speak to the Prosecution, the Prosecution would approach such person. If Bosnian authorities, let's say, arrest someone in two weeks time, in a month time and that person is available for us and willing to cooperate with us, we will file the motion and we will interview the witness, and we will ask the Chamber for leave to disclose this statement to the Defence. But other than that, we are not planning for the time being for the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. Apart from what was submitted in written filing, is there anything to add on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would seek to make a very brief observation arising from the questions that Your Honour asked from the Prosecutor, if I may. It may be that the answer to Your Honour's question was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks as if there will be further investigation. If looks as if there will be some more work done by the Prosecution. The impact that has on the Defence is unknown to us at this stage. It has a potential impact upon readiness for trial, upon resources, and upon other matters. We don't know what the impact is. I should indicate very keen not to delay matters and we are not looking to do so. If there are to be changes, it's very desirable that we be told of those immediately and as soon as possible and in a form that we can deal with. That applies both to new witness statements and to revisiting of previous witness statements. And I observe too, and finally, that there is a cumulative weight of such matters, that what may look like the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond occasional interview of a witness may be added to a weight of others. That concludes the remarks I wish to make about that. And I'm sorry, Your Honour. Did I understand you to seek whether there are any other matters that needed to be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Generally speaking? Thank you. Very well. Could I just place on record a couple of matters that are of relevance. Should we find - this is really a concession from the Defence or an offer, that should we find that our estimates as to trial length or any other matters are affected by rulings of the Chamber, we'll indicate that as soon as we can. We don't anticipate that that will be the case, but we wish to have the ability to be heard if that proves to be so. Your Honour, I mentioned that we've been provided with a great deal of assistance by the Prosecutor in terms of the witness statements and also exhibits, in electronic form, which has made our job much easier and made it much more likely that we would be ready, as we've indicated we are, and we wish to express our gratitude for that. An electronic disclosure suite has been made available to us as well. This would contain somewhere in the order of 11.000 documents. There is an order in place that the Prosecution provide an index in relation to it. That index is of great importance. It turns what is otherwise a massive, monstrous ignorance on our behalf into something that we can in fact use. We say that -- we submit that an index ought to consist of certain minimal requirements, and we say that those are that the document itself ought to be identified, firstly; secondly, the author of the document and any recipient of the document be identified; and finally, that some brief summary, even if it be a single line summary, be provided. The resources of the Defence are such that anything less is going to stretch our ability to use that material effectively, and although it's outside of the Court's ability to make any such order at this stage, we nevertheless want it to be made clear that that's what we think ought to exist. Your Honour's questions earlier have anticipated questions that we had and we have nothing to add to those. Those are the matters I would wish to raise at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow the first issue. You were asking about the trial length or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I was making the observation -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. As to the first observations I made, do you mean responding to what the -- to the Prosecutor's comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I make the comment that continued disclosure can disturb our plans and our estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can I hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just one issue with regard to this electronic disclosure suite. I hear the Defence says that the minimum requirement should be summary of which document, the name of the author of each document, and the name of those to whom document is addressed to. I read the Rule 66(B), I read Rule 66(A)(ii). I don't see this requirements in any rules in ICTY Rules of Procedure that require the Prosecution to not only disclose the document but also provide summary of those documents. I don't see this requirement. I don't see this obligation on the side of the Prosecution. Our obligation under 66(B) and 66 -- 68(ii), which is actually electronic form of 66(B), is that we're supposed to give the Defence access to the documents in our possession and control, not to provide a summary of each document, not to provide the names and other information about document but to provide access to the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tochilovsky, you are saying is that it is almost impossible on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yeah. If we had, let's say, 10, 20, a few dozens of documents it wouldn't be the issue. And we always, whenever we have opportunity, we meet the request from the Defence when we can do that, even if it goes beyond the Rules. For instance, just today we provided the Defence, as it was reported, the proper list of evidence, when you see the list of the exhibit, you click on the name of the exhibit and the exhibit appears on your screen. We provided that even we are not required to do that. But to do the same with thousands and thousands of documents in the electronic database, to provide summaries for all these documents, I don't see even any unit in ICTY which can do this job for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing this debate in every case. So Defence must have heard that too. Thank you. Is there any matter to be dealt with right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about Prosecutors? Is there any matter? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just one matter again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: One matter again. It may be just technical. We discussed that with the Defence. We will discuss that with the Defence later again. We have the practice in other Trial Chambers and, for instance, I have decision in Krajisnik case in front of me about the pre-trial brief where Judge of the Trial Chamber which received the case from pre-trial Chamber after almost two years. They issued the order, Scheduling Order for the filing of supplement to the pre-trial briefs. And in that order, the Trial Chamber with the Presiding Judge Orie they mentioned that given the length of time elapsed since the filing of the pre-trial briefs and the change of the Defence counsel, it is in the interest of justice to allow the parties to file a supplement to the pre-trial brief if they so wish. And of course in our case it is even more than two years. It's -- we filed our pre-trial brief and Defence filed their pre-trial brief in middle 2002, which now, for instance, speaking for the Prosecution, we are going through our pre-trial brief and check the ICTY's jurisprudence developed for this two and a half years, and there were changes in the jurisprudence. There were changes in application of some rules -- of some Articles of the ICTY cited. We now going through our pre-trial brief and to see whether there is any necessity to fine-tune the pre-trial brief and adjust it to current jurisprudence of the ICTY. At this time, again, we may be prompted like it happened in Krajisnik, by the Trial Chamber to submit, to refresh pre-trial brief. We may come to that conclusion after we review our pre-trial brief again in terms as I explained, and we may initiate also. But at this time what I want to do is just to notify the Defence, although we have already discussed that, that we may revisit this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I take that as the Prosecution's case may be reformulated in one way or another by new pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: As to the material facts, the charges, it's not going to change at all. It's based on the indictment and whatever pre-trial brief is - it's again, it is a rather fine-tuning rather than change of material facts. We are not going to change that. Change of the charges, we are not going to change that. The whole Prosecution theory, what is 7(3), what is command responsibility, failure to prevent, we are not going to change that. So there is nothing -- if, again, if we raise the issue on re-submission of the pre-trial brief because of the lapse of the time, it's not going to be any changes which would make the Defence impossible to meet the Prosecution case. It would be again fine-tuning rather than substantial changes in the material facts and charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, you will seek a leave from the Chamber to resubmit the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If we decide there is a need for that, of course we will seek the leave from the Chamber. But again, it's not the issue today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to hear from the Defence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, the answer to Your Honour's question, Your Honour's question being that the Prosecution case may be reformulated in one way or another by a new pre-trial brief. It appears the answer is yes. Can I indicate now that since we don't know in what terms that's going to be done, it would be mere words to respond, but I will indicate in advance that we would oppose that being done. It is appropriate for the Prosecutor to seek leave to do so, and we would seek leave to respond. Again, it's plain that such a reformulation may have consequences for the future of the trial. Whilst resources are a topic that the Trial Chamber is generally apt to avoid, and correctly so, it is an issue that weighs upon our minds in terms of how we prepare and whether we're able to prepare properly, whether we have equality of arms, whether we have appropriate time, whether we have been led by the state of the Prosecution case as it currently is to investigate particular areas which now no longer need to be investigated and upon which we have squandered our time and resources. What we submit is, therefore, that it is appropriate that leave be sought in writing, that we, the Defence, be entitled to respond in writing, that that be done in such a way as not to interfere with the potential starting time of the trial, and that whether or not those applications -- the Prosecution application focuses upon changes in the law or whether it involves what we - I put on record now - suspect is the case, that there will be some developments of a factual kind, those ought to be specified and pleaded with particularity so that we can respond in an informed and appropriate way at the relevant time. We make the final comment in response that the indictment is currently phrased, we submit, broadly, notwithstanding our failure to establish that in a previous motion that it was illicitly broad. It remains our submission that it still is broad. And that is also a context against which we have to prepare this case. We have to meet many allegations. And if the ground changes, it has the potential to prejudice the fair trial of the Defence. And for those reasons, we make the submissions that I've mentioned in anticipation of what we think is a certainty that the Prosecution will in fact seek that leave in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: First of all, just read transcript because I couldn't believe that Defence said that, that I stated that the whole case will be reformulated. I never said that. I don't know why it's in the transcript and why Defence alleged this. I never said that case will be reformulated, just opposite. I just said that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will see after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just fine-tuning, first of all. Secondly, I agree that it remains to be seen because it looks like Defence object to what it exist yet. Maybe we will never submit even or if we submit there will be no issues to challenge. So I think it's the objection, first of all, objection to what is not submitted is premature and secondly, again, I never said that the case will be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is premature at this moment, and once it is to be submitted, I would like to recommend to submit it as soon as possible. And if there's anything -- nothing further raised by the parties, hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
